title: Study: a bishop on its diagonal
author: Jean-Marc Loustau
teaser: A study post: today's own attempts did not pass the gate, so here is a prize-winner that does what they tried to do. Fifteen units, no flight. The bishop b6 stands where the knight d7 wants to give check. Every move of the bishop threatens the same mate. Ask which squares it may stop on, and what each of them spoils.

comment.what: A study post. Today's searches and hand constructions found no sound original (see How it was made), so the skill's fallback applies: an archive problem of the theme, with full credit. Loustau's 2nd Prize is a white correction of the fourth degree with changed mates. Every bishop move clears b6 for 2.Sb6#. The random moves leave the g1-a7 diagonal, and 1...Qxg1! puts the black queen on that diagonal, where it guards b6. The corrections stay on the diagonal between g1 and b6 and block it, but each blocks something a mate needs: on c5 the bishop stands on the mating square of 2.Qc5#, so 1...Bc7! (guarding b6) has no answer; on d4 it cuts the white queen from c5, so 1...Bc5! has none. On e3 the bishop blocks the diagonal and spoils nothing. The two bishop defences then get new mates, 2.Se7# and 2.Re5#, and 1...Qd4 gets 2.Qg8# instead of 2.Qxd4#. Our solver confirms the published solution, and the critique names the play as a white correction (1.B~? Qxg1! (4 moves); 1.Bc5? Bc7!; 1.Bd4? Bc5!; 1.Be3!).
flaws: The check 1...Qc4+ is answered by 2.dxc4#, a mate that captures the defender on its arrival square (E. Bourd, 14 Oct 2026: a minor flaw of construction). It is a by-play, not part of the correction.

Thirteen black moves that only allow the threat also allow a second mate (1...Rxf6 2.Sxf6#/Sb6#). These are random moves of the defence, not thematic variations, and the published solution leaves them out.
Fifteen units (8+7), with two black rooks and a black queen mostly there to keep White's force busy. Heavy, but the content is rich: three phases of correction and changed mates on the same defences.
This is not our work: it is published as a study, credited to its author, because today's original failed.
pluses: A full white correction: a random stage (four moves, one refutation), two corrections, each refuted differently, and the key as the last correction. Each correction answers the error of the stage before it and makes a new one.
The errors are line effects of one unit: the bishop's arrival square either takes a mating square (c5) or cuts the queen's line to it (d4). The critique reads both as white interference tries.
Changed mates: 1...Bc7 is met by 2.Qc5# in the random stage, by 2.Sxb4# after 1.Bd4? and by 2.Se7# after the key; 1...Bc5 by 2.Qxc5# and then 2.Re5#; 1...Qd4 by 2.Qxd4# and then 2.Qg8#.
No flight, a quiet key, a key piece in play, and one black unit (the bishop d6) supplies both correction refutations.
comment.process: Theme from the rotation: White correction, first time on the blog. About 150 minutes, about 80 solves and 24 search jobs, no sound original. (1) The kit had no search score for a white correction, so the run wrote one (chesscomp/compose/white_correction.py, used by evolve as WCORR=<square>) and checked it on two archive problems. (2) Eight evolve jobs from four sketches (a queen behind a bishop or a knight, the black king next to the mating square): four of the seeds already had a mate in one, which the new seed check in evolve reported at once instead of failing silently. (3) A bishop d3 masking the queen on the d-file: evolve grew 8/2K2R2/8/4k3/4PN1r/2RB4/2P4r/3Q4, 1.B~? Rd2!, 1.Be2! (the bishop closes the black rook's rank), a random stage and one correction only, with a diagram flight on d4 and no defence after the key. Eight more jobs never found a second correction. (4) By hand, a knight next to the black king (a knight next to the king can never check by moving, because of the colours) masking the queen's long diagonal: 8/6rb/1N1P4/4P3/1P1kNP2/8/1K2PP2/7Q gave 1.Sf6?/Sc3?/Sd2? Rg2! (the black rook interposes on the queen's line), and 1.Sg3!, which closes the g-file. But 1.Sg5 and 1.Sc5 also solve: the knight's landing squares next to the king's field give knight checks as second threats. Four more evolve jobs on that core found nothing better. (5) A rook-pair version on e4 with self-blocking interpositions had mates in one at once and was dropped at the time cap.
comment.lesson: In a white correction the corrections must answer the random refutation with a mate made by the key piece's new square, or by blocking the refuting line, and every correction square must spoil something of its own. Write that table first (for each arrival square: which defence it stops, which mate it spoils), then place the defenders. The searches here found the random stage and one correction at once, but never a second error: an error has to be designed, like a mate, before any search.

attempts.title: Bishop on the d-file: one correction (evolve, WCORR mode)
attempts.note: 1.B~ (Ba6, Bb5, Bc4, Bf1)? (2.Qd5#) but 1...Rd2!; 1.Be2! closes the second rank. Gate: FAIL, a diagram flight on d4 (fatal). After the key no Black move defends, and there is no second correction.

attempts.title: Knight next to the king: cooked
attempts.note: 1.Sf6?/Sc3?/Sd2? (2.Qd5#; after Sc3 and Sd2 also a knight check) but 1...Rg2!; 1.Sg3! closes the g-file. Gate: FAIL, cooked by 1.Sg5 (2.Se6#/Qd5#) and 1.Sc5; a dual after 1...Bg8 (2.Qe4#/Qd1#). The pawn d6 only stops 1.Sc5.

mentor_questions: In a white correction, is a random stage plus ONE correction (1.B~? Rd2!, 1.Be2!) a theme at all, or does it start only with two corrections refuted differently?

For a knight that masks a line next to the black king, the landing squares give knight checks, which become second threats in the tries and cooks in the solution. Is a bishop or rook the more natural key piece for a white correction, or would you keep the knight and stop the checks?
Loustau's random stage has four moves and one refutation, and the published solution lists them as 1.B~?. Is that the convention you use, or do you print one random try?
improvement: A white-correction score for the kit: chesscomp/compose/white_correction.py scores the moves of one White unit (a unique quiet key by it, a random refutation shared by at least two tries, distinct correction refutations, no king refutation, every thematic refutation answered in the key, changed mates rewarded). evolve uses it as WCORR=<square>, and also runs `python -m chesscomp.compose.white_correction FEN SQ`. Tested in tests/test_white_correction.py on Loustau (a hit) and Narayanan 1997 (no hit: a try refuted by a king move). evolve now also reports an illegal SEED (a check, a mate in one, promoted force) in its output instead of dying silently, which three earlier daily runs asked for.
